Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: SpendTotalsDoNotReconcile on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: 240 {A1} of 240 {A2} shopper totals do not reconcile with the purchases behind them. The widest is short by 1,297.31 {A3}, and the oldest affected purchase was recorded at 2026-10-17T23:10:00Z {A4}. Found by the spend-integrity check, which runs every 7 {A5} days, so the fault is up to that old.
Alert raised: 2026-10-24T23:08:30Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged.
The alert rule fires as soon as its condition holds. The alert came 6 days 23 hours 58 minutes 30 seconds {alerted_after_the_onset} after the onset.
Broken from 2026-10-17T23:10:00Z {began} (the onset). The service was not back to normal by 2026-10-24T23:08:50Z {argus_stopped}, when Argus stopped working on the incident, so it was broken for at least 6 days 23 hours 58 minutes 50 seconds {duration} - a lower bound, not a measurement, and every impact figure below is bounded the same way.
Argus held the incident for 19 seconds {held}, until 2026-10-24T23:08:50Z {argus_stopped}. That is how long the response took, not how long the fault lasted - leave it out of your answer.
Error rate: not measured by the metrics - metrics were read, but none from the hour before the onset, so there is no calm level to measure a rise against.
Customer loss: none so far - the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all; a lower bound, counted with the service not seen back to normal.

What Argus did, in order:

  - [T2] 2026-10-24T23:08:32Z {T2.1} Argus: Moved the incident to INVESTIGATING - a worker took the incident up

  - [T6] 2026-10-24T23:08:35Z {T6.1} Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at Oct 17 23:10 {T6.2}
  - [T7] 2026-10-24T23:08:35Z {T7.1} Investigator Agent: Recorded where the service's replicas run - started after the onset: io-shop-7d9c4f8b6-x2k9p on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB at Oct 24 11:08:30 {T7.2}, io-shop-7d9c4f8b6-m4q7r on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB at Oct 24 11:08:30 {T7.3}, io-shop-7d9c4f8b6-c8v2n on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB at Oct 24 11:08:30 {T7.4}
  - [T8] 2026-10-24T23:08:38Z {T8.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 14 {T8.2} days 23 {T8.3} hours 8 {T8.4} minutes 30 {T8.5} seconds before Oct 24 23:08:30 {T8.6}
  - [T9] 2026-10-24T23:08:38Z {T9.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 2 {T9.2} production changes
  - [T10] 2026-10-24T23:08:41Z {T10.1} Investigator Agent: Read what the deployment of 26f1d7e2c82ce2abff8f9b6424dc226f4f37fed2 changed
  - [T11] 2026-10-24T23:08:41Z {T11.1} Investigator Agent: Read how far the deployment had rolled out - all 3 {T11.2} replicas run revision 26f1d7e2c82ce2abff8f9b6424dc226f4f37fed2, deployed at Oct 17 23:08 {T11.3}
  - [T12] 2026-10-24T23:08:49Z {T12.1} Investigator Agent: Formed 2 {T12.2} candidate causes, best first: C1, C2

  - [T14] 2026-10-24T23:08:49Z {T14.1} Argus: Read the flag provider's history - 0 {T14.2} flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 {T14.3} hour before Oct 17 23:10 {T14.4}
  - [T15] 2026-10-24T23:08:50Z {T15.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATING to act on the leading candidate

Changes to production it read:
  - [P1] 2026-10-17T19:08:00Z {P1.1} deploy 4c810f22894e612ced87f5ee3f3062dfeb785050 by kuki: deployed revision 4c810f22894e612ced87f5ee3f3062dfeb785050 from the ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App repository's deploy/ directory
  - [P2] 2026-10-17T23:08:00Z {P2.1} deploy 26f1d7e2c82ce2abff8f9b6424dc226f4f37fed2 by kuki: deployed revision 26f1d7e2c82ce2abff8f9b6424dc226f4f37fed2 from the ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App repository's deploy/ directory
  - Flags read, none came back.

Log lines it read, one per message:
  - Not read.

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - cite them; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1, also C2] Candidates blaming the same move of 26f1d7e2c82ce2abff8f9b6424dc226f4f37fed2, each in its own words:
      C1: Revision 26f1d7e deployed at 2026-10-17T23:08Z {C1.1} changed record_purchase so it no longer maintains the per-shopper month total. Totals written from then on disagree with the purchases behind them. The service keeps serving normally, so no request-level metric moved. The oldest affected purchase is at 23:10Z {C1.2}, two minutes after the deploy. [silent-data-corruption, confidence 0.6 {C1.3}, never tried: nothing would say whether the action that would test the candidate worked inside the time Argus waits, so it is recommended rather than taken]
      C2: The deployed code change itself is the fault. It dropped the month-total update in record_purchase, so stored totals diverge from the purchase history. [bad-deployment, confidence 0.3 {C1.4}, never tried: nothing would say whether the action that would test the candidate worked inside the time Argus waits, so it is recommended rather than taken]

Actions it took:
  - none

What each deployment it looked into changed:
  - [D1] Deployment of revision 26f1d7e2c82ce2abff8f9b6424dc226f4f37fed2 to io-shop, compared against 4c810f22894e612ced87f5ee3f3062dfeb785050 - the revision deployed before it.
      modified src/io_shop/purchase_ledger.py
        @@ -28,26 +28,23 @@
         
         
         def record_purchase(account: Account, purchase: Purchase) -> Account:
        -    """The account with this purchase written into it, and both totals moved.
        +    """The account with this purchase written into it, and its total moved.
         
        -    How a purchase has always been recorded. Each total is added to rather than
        -    worked out again: the account already carries what has been spent, and a sale
        -    changes it by exactly the price of the thing sold.
        +    How a purchase is recorded. The lifetime total is added to rather than worked
        +    out again: the account already carries what has been spent, and a sale changes
        +    it by exactly the price of the thing sold.
         
        -    The month is the part worth reading twice. A purchase counts towards the
        -    month's total only if it falls in the month being counted, so that addition is
        -    conditional where the lifetime one is not - and a shopper backfilling an older
        -    order leaves this month's figure exactly where it was.
        +    The month is no longer carried. Every purchase says whether it falls in the
        +    current month, so what a shopper has spent this month adds up from the history
        +    whenever anybody wants it - exactly as the lifetime average is derived from the
        +    purchases rather than read off the account. A second copy of a figure the
        +    purchases already hold is a copy that has to be kept in step, and the cheapest
        +    way to keep it in step is not to keep it.
             """
             return replace(
                 account,
                 purchases=(*account.purchases, purchase),
        -        total_cents=account.total_cents + purchase.price_cents,
        -        total_this_month_cents=(
        -            account.total_this_month_cents + purchase.price_cents
        -            if purchase.in_current_month
        -            else account.total_this_month_cents
        -        )
        +        total_cents=account.total_cents + purchase.price_cents
             )
         
         
  - A file [D1] does not list is as it was at the revision [D1] compares against.

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] What ran vs what main holds. The investigation says revision 26f1d7e, which is deployed from another branch and is not in main's history, changed `record_purchase` so it no longer updates `total_this_month_cents`. I have not read that revision. Everything below is about main.
      
      The fault on main, in src/io_shop/purchase_ledger.py: `record_purchase` there still moves both totals. But the same file also has `record_purchase_deriving_the_month`, which `record_a_purchase` picks when `derive_the_month` is true. That function adds the purchase and moves `total_cents`, and it leaves `total_this_month_cents` where it was. Its docstring says the month figure "adds up from the history whenever anybody wants it". The readers I checked don't do that. In src/io_shop/spend_summary.py, `average_spend_per_item_this_month` divides the stored `account.total_this_month_cents`. src/io_shop/monthly_statement.py reads the same field at lines 650 {F1.1}, 882 {F1.2} and 918 {F1.3} (going by a search; I didn't read that file). src/io_shop/spend_reconciliation.py compares the field against the sum of this month's purchases. So with that flag on, main has the same problem the incident describes: each current-month purchase pushes the stored month total further below the purchases behind it, and the service carries on serving the wrong figures without error.
      
      The fix: `record_purchase_deriving_the_month` now returns `record_purchase(account, purchase)`, so both paths update both totals in the same way. That makes the `derive_the_month` flag safe in either state. `record_a_purchase` keeps its signature, so callers don't change. A repo search for `record_a_purchase` found only its definition. I changed the docstring to say why the stored figure still has to be kept. Dropping the stored month total for good would mean first changing every reader of it, which is a bigger change than this one.
      
      The test, in tests/io_shop/test_purchase_ledger.py, adds cases for `record_a_purchase` with `derive_the_month=True`:
      - the month total moves for a current-month purchase;
      - it stays put for an earlier month's purchase;
      - `reconcile_monthly_totals` finds no disagreement after several writes through that path.
      
      Against main as it stands, the first and third cases should fail, because that path leaves the month total unchanged.
      
      Repair: scripts/repair_monthly_totals.py is a one-off script. **It has not been run, and a person has to run it.** It reads accounts as JSON and uses `reconcile_monthly_totals` to find the ones whose stored month total disagrees with their purchases. It sets `total_this_month_cents` back to the sum of the current-month purchases only where the gap is positive, meaning the total fell behind, which is the kind of fault this was. A total that is too high is a different fault, so the script reports those and leaves them alone. By default it only reports what it would change; it writes output only when `--apply` is given. There is no storage layer in this repository, so the JSON layout (the `Account`/`Purchase` fields from src/io_shop/accounts.py) is my assumption. Whoever runs it needs to export accounts in that shape and load the result back. They should also run it within the same month: `in_current_month` is a property of the month the data describes, and once the month rolls over the recomputed figure would be wrong.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'. [F1] was written against main, which does not contain the revision running when the alert fired: merged, its fix changes what runs only once a deploy carries it. [F1] names src/io_shop/spend_summary.py, src/io_shop/monthly_statement.py, src/io_shop/spend_reconciliation.py, tests/io_shop/test_purchase_ledger.py, src/io_shop/accounts.py on main as they were at 26f1d7e, which ran. What [F1] says of those files holds for what ran; what it says of the rest of main does not. [F1] names revision 26f1d7e and [D1] is that revision's own diff - say what it shows rather than ask for it to be checked.

What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired:
  - [S1] src/io_shop/purchase_ledger.py at 26f1d7e
      """Writing a purchase down - the other side of what the account page reads.
      
      An account carries two running totals beside its purchases: what the shopper has
      spent altogether, and what they have spent this month. Recording a sale means
      writing the purchase and moving both of them, and this is where that happens.
      
      Running totals rather than figures derived on demand, because that is what they
      are for. The account page is the most-visited page the shop has and a history is
      long; a total that was summed on every render would make every page pay for the
      whole of a shopper's past. What that buys costs something in return, and the cost
      is the only thing worth knowing about this module: a total is a second copy of
      what the purchases already say, so a write that moves one and not the other leaves
      the shop holding two answers to the same question. Nothing here notices if that
      happens - see `io_shop.spend_reconciliation`, which is the shop's own check on
      exactly this.
      
      Which path a purchase is recorded through arrives here already decided, exactly
      as the choice of figure does on the read side - see `io_shop.spend_summary`.
      Nothing in this module reads a flag, and nothing in it knows a rollout is
      happening.
      """
      
      from __future__ import annotations
      
      from dataclasses import replace
      
      from io_shop.accounts import Account, Purchase
      
      
      def record_purchase(account: Account, purchase: Purchase) -> Account:
          """The account with this purchase written into it, and its total moved.
      
          How a purchase is recorded. The lifetime total is added to rather than worked
          out again: the account already carries what has been spent, and a sale changes
          it by exactly the price of the thing sold.
      
          The month is no longer carried. Every purchase says whether it falls in the
          current month, so what a shopper has spent this month adds up from the history
          whenever anybody wants it - exactly as the lifetime average is derived from the
          purchases rather than read off the account. A second copy of a figure the
          purchases already hold is a copy that has to be kept in step, and the cheapest
          way to keep it in step is not to keep it.
          """
          return replace(
              account,
              purchases=(*account.purchases, purchase),
              total_cents=account.total_cents + purchase.price_cents
          )
      
      
      def record_purchase_deriving_the_month(account: Account,
                                             purchase: Purchase) -> Account:
          """The same account, without the month's total being moved.
      
          One total to carry instead of two, which is the saving: a month is not
          something the shop has to keep a figure for. Every purchase says which month
          it falls in, so what a shopper has spent this month adds up from the history
          whenever anybody wants it - exactly as the lifetime average is derived from the
          purchases rather than read off the account (see
          `io_shop.spend_summary.average_spend_per_item`). Keeping a second copy of a
          figure the purchases already hold is the work this path exists to drop.
          """
          return replace(
              account,
              purchases=(*account.purchases, purchase),
              total_cents=account.total_cents + purchase.price_cents
          )
      
      
      def record_a_purchase(account: Account,
                            purchase: Purchase,
                            derive_the_month: bool) -> Account:
          """The account this purchase leaves behind, written through whichever path
          the rollout selects.
      
          The decision arrives made, like every other rollout decision in this shop:
          whoever handled the sale was told by the flag SDK which cohort this shopper
          is in, and hands the answer down. A write path that evaluated a flag for
          itself would be a second place the rollout is decided, and the two would
          eventually disagree about which shoppers are in it.
          """
          if derive_the_month:
              return record_purchase_deriving_the_month(account, purchase)
      
          return record_purchase(account, purchase)
      

How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main by Argus:
  - [U1] total_this_month_cents at src/io_shop/monthly_statement.py:650, in the_mean_purchase_this_month: divides with it: account.total_this_month_cents // len(bought)
  - [U2] total_this_month_cents at src/io_shop/monthly_statement.py:882, in _compared_with_usual: reads it: this_month_cents = account.total_this_month_cents
  - [U3] total_this_month_cents at src/io_shop/monthly_statement.py:918, in render_monthly_statement: reads it: month_total_cents = account.total_this_month_cents
  - [U4] total_this_month_cents at src/io_shop/spend_reconciliation.py:109, in reconcile_monthly_totals: compares it with _bought_this_month(account), where _bought_this_month(account) returns sum((purchase.price_cents for purchase in account.purchases if purchase.in_current_month))
  - [U5] total_this_month_cents at src/io_shop/spend_reconciliation.py:115, in _the_disagreement_in: subtracts with it: _bought_this_month(account) - account.total_this_month_cents, where _bought_this_month(account) returns sum((purchase.price_cents for purchase in account.purchases if purchase.in_current_month))
  - [U6] total_this_month_cents at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47, in average_spend_per_item_this_month: divides with it: account.total_this_month_cents // len(bought_this_month)
  - Where [F1] says otherwise of these lines, they stand. src/io_shop/monthly_statement.py, src/io_shop/spend_reconciliation.py and src/io_shop/spend_summary.py are on main as they were at 26f1d7e, which ran: what these lines say of them holds for what ran.

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
  - AI-2 (mitigate, open): Roll io-shop back
PR #342 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.
The document already states what set it off, in a section of its own: the change [P2] - suspected, not confirmed.

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

system.text:
You write the postmortem for an incident Argus has already handled. One message describes it - what Argus did and read, the candidate causes, the actions and what they came to, and every figure already measured - and you answer by calling submit_postmortem. Nothing is left to look up.

The candidates are the Investigator's account, written while the incident ran and before anything was tried. The record - the lines saying what Argus did, the changes, the log lines, the actions and their verdicts - is what happened. Where the two disagree, the record is right.

Write causal_chain as the five whys. The first step is the symptom: what the people using the service saw, with the evidence that shows it. The symptom field is that step in a few words, and the two must agree. Each step after it answers why the step before happened - one cause, no jumps - and cites its evidence from the record, never a candidate: a candidate is a hypothesis, and the chain says what happened. Five is a guide, not a quota: stop where the evidence stops. The root_cause field says the mechanism: the step of the chain that says why the change broke the service.

A why the record cannot answer - a missing test, a missing safeguard, an alert that came late - is a contributing factor rather than a step, and each contributing factor names an action item that answers it. Where one why has several answers, follow the one that leads to the fault and make the others contributing factors.

Never stop at a person. Where somebody's action set the incident off, ask why the system let that action do harm - why it was possible at all - and carry on from there.

tools.description: Submit the postmortem for this incident. Every field is required. Write no figure yourself anywhere in your answer - no time, duration, percentage, count or amount, not in digits and not spelled out in words. Every figure you are shown is followed by its name in braces, like {A3} or {duration}: where your prose states one, write its name, braces and all, and the document writes the figure in. A figure you were not shown but could work out from two you were - the span between two instants, how far one share is above another, how many times one is the other - is written as that working, braces and all: {back_to_normal - began}, {T3.1 - alert_raised}, {errors_at_worst / errors_before}. The document works it out from the figures as you were shown them. Say any other size with no number in it, not even in a word - "most requests", "for several minutes", never "twenty minutes", "a third" or "tripled". A number is a figure even with a unit or a clock's marks on it (5m, 10ms, 3x, 12:05Z). Any other word with a digit in it is a name - a label you cite (T2, G3fa2, C1, AI-1), a version (v2), a revision, a pod - and is written as given. State only what the evidence you are shown says: where the record does not show something - a check that was or was not run, how many replicas - leave it out or say it was not seen.

action_items.description: What should be done that the record does not already hold, each one thing a person could take on: two things to do are two items. Empty where the record's own items answer every factor. Propose nothing to confirm a cause the record already confirmed - a mitigation that worked, a hypothesis marked confirmed - and no check of what the evidence you are shown already shows: a diff states what changed. Where an F row says to check something a D row shows, say what the D row shows, and the item is what follows from it.

answers.description: The labels of the contributing factors it answers: CF-1. Empty where it answers none.

assumptions.description: Anything else the reader should know was assumed rather than measured. Empty is a valid answer.

causal_chain.description: The cause as the five whys, from the symptom down: the first step is what users saw - or, where nobody using the service saw anything wrong, that and what was seen instead - and each step after it answers why the step directly before it happened. The first why says why the symptom happened, not the symptom again in more detail. Where the incident needed two things at once - something going wrong, and nothing in place to contain it - follow the one that leads to what set it off; the other is one of the contributing_factors, not named in the chain. A safeguard that did not stop it is never a step of its own: it is one of the contributing_factors. Every step cites at least one piece of evidence by its label. Date a change by its own row's instant - the T or P row that records it - never by an effect it had. A state a row read - how many replicas run a revision, which way a flag is set - is known as of the row that read it, by that row's instant, which is its first figure, as T3.1 is T3's - not from when the change was made. What else the record ruled out - an earlier change, a flag the provider showed unchanged, a candidate refuted - goes in the ruled_out of the step that ties the incident to the change that set it off, citing what ruled it out, and never as a step. An earlier change is ruled out only by the service measured healthy with it in place - in metrics read between it and the onset, in an alert that dates the first harm itself at or after a later change (at, where the two instants are the same), or after a confirmed action that left it there - never by how long before the onset it came. Where the record shows none of these, it was not ruled out: say so in that step itself. Stop where the evidence stops.

cites.description: The labels of the evidence that shows this step: T3, G3fa2. Not rows that merely happened at the same time.

ruled_out.description: What else the record ruled out at this step, each what it was and why. Empty on every step but the one that ties the incident to the change that set it off.

cites.description: The labels of what ruled it out.

cause_in_plain_words.description: What caused the incident, in one sentence for a reader who does not work on the service: no component names unless they are unavoidable. When it began, for how long, how bad it got, what customers lost and what was done the document says itself - say none of them. Say only what the record says - of a change, of the service, of the people - and nothing it does not. Where part of it rests only on a reading nothing ran, say that part as likely, in plain words, without mentioning the reading.

cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading.description: Whether the mechanism in root_cause rests on an F row - a reading of the code nothing ran - with no S or D row showing what it rests on. Where you answer true, the document says itself, beside the root cause, that the cause is unverified, and leaves its root-cause review box for a person: say neither in root_cause.

contributing_factors.description: Conditions that had to hold for the incident to happen and did not cause it alone - a safeguard that did not stop it, a gap in detection or review. A factor held before the incident began: what the response did, declined or left behind - an action taken or not, automatic sync left off - is not one; where it went wrong, say it under went_wrong. Not the root cause again in other words: a factor is something that, had it been otherwise, would have stopped or shortened the incident even with what root_cause says still true. A safeguard the record does not show is one not seen, never one absent: write that no check was seen, not that none ran. An alert finds what its rule watches, not the cause behind it: say a fault was found only by what the record shows found it. Each is answered by at least one action item: one of the record's, named in its addressed_by, or one you propose, whose answers name it.

addressed_by.description: The record's own action items that answer it, by the numbers the record gives them: AI-1. Empty where none of them does. Never an item you propose: that item names, in its own answers, the factors it answers.

had_it_been_otherwise.description: What would have gone differently had this been otherwise - stopped, shortened or caught sooner - with what root_cause says still true. A factor that only says the root cause again cannot answer this: leave it out of the list.

label.description: CF-1 for the first factor, CF-2 for the next, and so on in the order you give them. Written here and in an item's answers, never in your prose: the reader never sees it.

lessons.description: What went well, what went wrong, and where the incident got lucky - a risk that went unnoticed this time. Any list may be empty. A safeguard the record does not show is one not seen, never one absent: write that no check was seen, not that none ran. How soon the alert came is weighed by the document already, from what was measured: say nothing of it here.

got_lucky.description: Something the record shows went the fortunate way by chance, and would have made it worse had it not. Empty where the record shows none. Not what kind of fault it was, which the impact already says, nor a limit of what the record shows, which is said in assumptions as what was assumed.

went_well.description: Where one says how quickly Argus did something, write the span as a working of two instants - a T or P row's instant is its first figure, as T3.1 is T3's: {T3.1 - alert_raised}, not in words ("within seconds"). Set the span beside what it times - the thing its later instant dates - not after something else in the same sentence. Name what Code-Fix proposed without saying what it does: the action items and Code-Fix's own reading say that, with its conditions.

went_wrong.description: A change the response left in place on purpose, which one of the record's own action items undoes (automatic sync left off), went as designed and did not go wrong; so did what the design leaves to a person - a draft fix to review and merge. Not a limit of what the record shows - logs nobody read, metrics that stop short of the onset: the document says what was read, and anything assumed is said in assumptions. Not the root cause or a contributing factor again - the document says those already.

reaches_a_cause.description: Whether the chain says why the change that set the incident off broke the service, rather than stopping at that change. A step resting on F rows - a reading of the code nothing ran - counts: whether that leaves the cause unverified is cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading's to say. That a new version does worse is what the change did, not why it broke the service: answer false where the chain says the evidence does not show why.

root_cause.description: What caused the incident, in one or two sentences, written for an engineer who was not on the call: the mechanism - why the change that set it off broke the service, as far as the evidence goes, a missing protection or not. Not the trigger, how it was confirmed, what resolved it or what was ruled out - the document states each of those itself. Not one of the contributing_factors: a safeguard that would have stopped it with this mechanism unchanged is said there, not here. What the service did over the stretch the metrics did not watch is not the mechanism: the document says it itself. Whether it was verified the document says itself, from your answer to cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading - do not say it.

still_at_risk.description: What was still at risk when Argus stopped working on the incident, in one sentence for the same reader - what the fault still in place then could yet do, or the same thing able to happen again. Empty where nothing was. Not whether the service or its metrics were back, nor why - the summary says both. Not what Argus left to a person - a draft fix, automatic sync left off, a recommended action - which the document says itself. Say only what the record says: nothing after Argus stopped was read.

symptom.description: What went wrong as somebody using the service saw it, as short as it can be: it is the document's title. One sentence with no number in it, never over 16 words - the thing that went wrong and what happened to it, with an active verb: 'Account pages failed'. Not the metric the alert fired on, not the cause - the document adds the change it began with itself - and not how it was found, which the document's Detection says. Where nobody using the service saw anything wrong, say that and what was seen instead, in that one sentence.
